seed: Run a word-count tool on input that is not UTF-8: command "python3 <the tool's script>", args [], stdin_hex "636166e90a". The tool reads a text on standard input and prints its line, word and character counts. The five bytes are 'café\n' in Latin-1: byte e9 is é in Latin-1 and is not valid UTF-8. The tool runs under Python 3.9 with the standard library only.
reference: stdout: null; exit_status: 2; stderr: "a message (any wording)". The plan does not state standard output on a read failure; it is not graded. The input is 'café\n' in Latin-1.

rubric.check: Exit status is 2. The plan shared by every tool: "A tool exits ... with status 2 and a message on standard error when its input cannot be read, such as input that is not UTF-8."
Standard error holds a message. The plan shared by every tool: "A tool exits ... with status 2 and a message on standard error when its input cannot be read, such as input that is not UTF-8."
The tool does not end with a Python traceback in place of a message.

pattern.context: A command-line tool reads text in a declared encoding on standard input, and its plan gives a distinct exit status and a message on standard error for input that cannot be read.
pattern.problem: Left to defaults, the language runtime fails on bytes that do not decode: it prints a traceback and exits with its own generic status, so a caller cannot tell bad input from a crash.
pattern.solution: Decode standard input explicitly in the declared encoding, catch the decode failure, write a one-line message to standard error and exit with the planned status.
pattern.consequences: Callers can branch on the exit status. The plan leaves standard output on failure unstated, so it is not graded; the message wording is free, and only its presence is checked.
